title: The Call for Analog Assessments: Let Teachers Teach
author: Martina Meijer
source: firstfish.substack.com (First Fish Chronicles, guest essay), October 26, 2026
summary: This guest essay for Emily Cherkin's First Fish Chronicles, by New York City teacher Martina Meijer, argues that districts should return to paper-based assessments. Meijer connects NYC's mandated curricula and computer-based screeners such as i-Ready to private-equity ownership of the curriculum and testing companies, and says the data mainly serves district staff who want top-down monitoring. She contends that experienced teachers already know what the screeners flag, so the tests drain instructional time while undermining educator expertise. She cites research that students comprehend and retain more from paper than from screens, and that handwriting aids memory. She notes that the justification that state tests are now digital ignores that typing is not taught and that third-grade scores fell in the first year of statewide computer-based testing. Her conclusion is that districts should center student and teacher needs, and she credits parent and educator organizing for slowing the push toward AI and screens.
points: Meijer argues that computer-based screeners serve district staff who want comparison data and control, not the children being tested.
She points to private-equity and venture ownership of curricula, screeners, and state test publishers as a driver of the push toward digital assessment.
Teachers already know the needs that tools like i-Ready flag, so the tests add little information while signaling distrust of educator judgment.
Research on reading on paper and note-taking by hand supports analog assessment, yet districts claim that digital state tests force digital everything.
Digital testing is mandated without time to teach typing, and statewide third-grade scores dropped in the first year of computer-based testing.
quotes: Superintendents are not centering the needs of the children in their district when they mandate computer-based testing. They are centering the comfort and ease of district staff.

Despite this data being redundant to what educators already gather in their classrooms, district staff have become reliant on access to this school- and student-level data to define their jobs’ relevance and maintain a top-down sense of control over and monitoring of school staff.

Teachers watched as the AFT and UFT unions partnered with OpenAI and Google to support NYDOE ushering in AI use. Through organizing and advocacy, the AIM Coalition was able to achieve a one-year curbing (we can’t call it a moratorium due to the numerous carve-outs) of AI use and screen use, which was a remarkable thing!

As an educator in 2026, I see the need for students to read whole physical books of their choice, and the need for students to take tests and write essays on paper. The efficacy of analog modes of learning is supported by the data.
Educators are continuously assessing their students, whether formally or informally. Computer-based assessments do not add any new information. In fact, they serve to undermine educator expertise.
I have yet to meet an educator who was not already aware of a child’s needs that were flagged by i-Ready.

But despite this argument, superintendents are not making typing or computer literacy a priority for students to learn at any age. There is no time allotted for teaching students how to type, but they are expected to produce a typed essay.

The level of distrust towards educators, the lack of creativity and autonomy, and the removal of joy from the classroom through overassessment and overly prescriptive curricular materials is contributing to experienced, talented educators leaving the profession.
